L: In 2031 Laura shows co-sponsors her broker's own statement of the account that holds the building's Treasuries, with what they will pay by December 2032 set beside what they are worth that day. She also gives them a pledge letter she has signed, for $115,000 on today's figures, with its purpose and its date: the statement shows the money exists, the letter says it will be given, and a letter is what a funder's gift office can count. In October 2007 Lehman Brothers itself pledged $10 million to Spelman College over five years, to be paid from the bank's own future money; when the bank failed in 2008, the college received $3 million of it. Laura's money is held for her before she signs.

In 2033 I am opening a creative residency in Taiwan, where artists, writers, designers and educators can live and work for a time. I believe stories change how people see the world, and I want storytellers to have room to tell them.

My contribution to the building will be between $95,000 and $115,000. The $95,000 has been held for me in US Treasuries since January 2028. The $115,000 has been held since January 2031, when I moved half my shares into Treasuries. The $95,000 is the part that never depended on my shares. Since January 2031 neither figure depends on them, so no market can change either one. Treasuries are guaranteed by the US government and pay exactly what they promise.

I sign for the top because the shares I moved in January 2031 were always meant for the building. My letter fixes the sum at $115,000. If the fund holding these Treasuries pays out less, I will make up the difference myself, from money I kept back. The letter is in US dollars, with its Taiwan-dollar value on the day I sign it in 2031. The amount in Taiwan dollars will depend on the exchange rate on the day it is paid, in January 2033.

My whole commitment has two parts: $50,000 a year for the residency's running costs from 2033 to 2042, and $115,000 for the building. Together they make $615,000 in all. I began buying the Treasuries for the yearly payments in January 2027 and finished in January 2028. I am committing in writing now, in 2031, without waiting for anyone to match me. The $115,000 will be paid in January 2033.
NOTES: Hardest was "why Taiwan": the case says who the residency serves and that Laura believes stories change how people see the world, but gives no reason for Taiwan, so her words name the place without inventing one. The currency sentence names the day she signs in 2031 rather than quoting the 6 November 2026 rate, because a 2026 rate spoken in 2031 would puzzle a funder; the letter itself would print the figure (about NT$3.77 million at 32.768 to the dollar on today's figures). To keep near 230 words I cut a sentence saying the half of her shares kept back is untouched by giving the top, so "money I kept back" arrives a little unexplained; with more room it goes back in, straight after "I sign for the top". I would also test "no market can change either one" against the make-up promise two sentences later, since a careful funder may ask why the promise is needed if nothing can change the figure.
